sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A **datasheet** is the contract between an op-amp maker and you. Learning to read one means knowing which numbers bound which errors, and which conditions they were measured under.

Key entries: **open-loop gain** (often in dB) sets static gain error; **GBW** sets closed-loop bandwidth; **slew rate** limits large fast signals; **offset voltage** and **bias currents** set DC errors; **noise density** sets the noise floor; **CMRR** and **PSRR** tell how well the part ignores common-mode and supply changes; the **input common-mode range** and **output swing** tell which voltages actually work. Always check the typical versus maximum columns and the test conditions (supply, load, temperature).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
dB to ratio: \(A = 10^{A_{dB}/20}\)
Closed-loop bandwidth: \(BW \approx \dfrac{GBW}{1/f}\)
Full-power bandwidth: \(f_{FP} = \dfrac{SR}{2\pi V_p}\)
Output offset: \(V_{os}\,(1 + R_2/R_1) + I_{OS}R_2\) (with bias compensation)

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A part lists \(A_{OL} = 100\ \mathrm{dB}\), \(GBW = 10\ \mathrm{MHz}\), \(SR = 5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\), \(V_{os,max} = 0.5\ \mathrm{mV}\). For a gain-of-20 amplifier with a 5 V peak output:
- \(A_{OL} = 10^5\), static error \(\approx 20/10^5 = 0.02\%\).
- \(BW \approx 10\ \mathrm{MHz}/20 = 500\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
- \(f_{FP} = 5\times10^6/(2\pi\times5) \approx 159\ \mathrm{kHz}\): slewing limits full-swing signals first.
- Output offset up to \(20\times0.5 = 10\ \mathrm{mV}\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Reading a "typical" value as guaranteed.
- Converting dB with 10 instead of 20.
- Ignoring the input common-mode range: an input near a rail may not work.
- Forgetting that specs depend on the stated supply and load.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: This skill pulls the whole op-amp chapter together. Real design is choosing the cheapest part whose worst-case specs meet the requirements, and checking each error budget as above.
